opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. So, being on the Bard team was a really formative experience. I was at Google for a long time before that, working on things like recommendation systems and later on large language models, and when Bard came together it was this very intense, all-hands kind of effort. One of the things that became really clear to me during that time was just how central data is to everything. People tend to talk about model architectures and compute, and those obviously matter, but a huge fraction of the actual work, and a huge fraction of the gains we were seeing, came down to the data: how you curate it, how you generate it, how you clean it, how you evaluate what you have.

And at a place like Google, you have enormous resources to throw at that problem. You have teams of people, internal tooling, lots of infrastructure for building and filtering datasets for post-training, for instruction tuning, for evaluation. But when I looked outside, I realized most companies don't have anything close to that. They want to customize models for their own use cases, maybe fine-tune a smaller model, or build an agent that works reliably in their domain, and the bottleneck almost always ends up being the data. They don't have good training data, they don't have good evals, and they don't have the tooling to create them efficiently.

So the thesis for Bespoke Labs really came out of that. If data curation is the thing that separates a mediocre model from a great one, then there should be tools and platforms that make that process accessible to everyone, not just the big frontier labs. That's where things like Curator came from, our open-source library for synthetic data generation and curation, and also some of the reasoning model work we did, like the Bespoke-Stratos and later the OpenThoughts collaboration, where we showed that with carefully curated data you can get really strong reasoning performance out of relatively small models.

So in a sense, Bard taught me that data is the lever, and Bespoke Labs is about putting that lever in more people's hands.

r001.rationale: The response says a huge fraction of Bard’s work and gains came from data curation, generation, cleaning, and evaluation.

r002.rationale: It says most companies lack Google’s internal tooling and infrastructure for building and filtering datasets, motivating Bespoke Labs.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes data’s importance but does not compare improving training data with tuning model hyperparameters.

r004.rationale: It does not describe DataComp or an approach that holds the model fixed while optimizing data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So I was at Google for about nine years, and the last chunk of that was on the Bard team, which was really the first time I was working on the post-training side of large language models at scale. Before that I'd been in recommender systems, working on things like YouTube and the reinforcement learning work for recommendations, so I'd spent a long time thinking about data and how it shapes model behavior.

What struck me on Bard was how much of the actual progress came down to data rather than architecture. The model architecture was more or less fixed. The compute budget was more or less fixed. What moved the needle week to week was the quality of the supervised fine-tuning data, the preference data, how well the eval sets reflected what users actually cared about. And a surprising amount of the team's effort went into just curating that, writing instructions for raters, filtering out bad examples, figuring out which synthetic data pipelines actually helped and which ones quietly hurt the model.

The other thing I saw was that the tooling for all of this was pretty ad hoc, even inside Google. Lots of one-off scripts, lots of tribal knowledge. If you were a team outside the frontier labs trying to do the same thing, you basically had nothing. People would throw a generic dataset at a fine-tuning job and be disappointed with the result, without really understanding that the data was the problem.

So the thesis for Bespoke Labs came out of those two observations together. Data curation is the real lever for making models good at a specific task, and almost nobody outside a handful of labs has good tooling or know-how for it. We wanted to make it possible for any team to build high-quality, task-specific datasets, both synthetic and curated, and then train small models that genuinely compete with much larger general-purpose ones on their particular problem. That's what led to things like our open-source Curator library and the Bespoke-Stratos and MiniCheck work. The bet is that the frontier is going to keep moving, but for most real applications, the thing that determines whether your model works is whether you got the data right.

r001.rationale: The response says Bard’s week-to-week progress depended on data quality, curation, and evaluation, while the model architecture and compute budget stayed largely fixed.

r002.rationale: It describes Google’s tooling as ad hoc and says teams outside frontier labs lacked comparable tools and know-how, motivating Bespoke Labs.

r003.rationale: It says data quality moved the needle while architecture and compute were fixed, but does not compare data improvements with tuning model hyperparameters.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe DataComp or its method of holding the model fixed while optimizing data.

astra-6.text:
The big takeaway for me was how much the data matters. It’s easy to focus on the model, but building a useful application also means figuring out what you want it to do, getting the right examples, and evaluating whether it’s actually improving.

That’s the thesis behind Bespoke Labs: help teams turn their domain knowledge into data they can use to build and improve AI systems. A general-purpose model gives you a starting point, but the opportunity is in making it work really well for your particular task.

sol-6.1.text:
Working on Bard gave me a firsthand appreciation for how much the quality of the data matters. You can have a very capable base model, but getting it to behave the way you want depends on the examples you train it on and how you evaluate the results.

That shaped our thesis for Bespoke Labs: a lot of the opportunity is in helping teams turn their domain knowledge into high-quality training data. Each company has different tasks and a different definition of a good answer. We wanted to make that process of creating data, evaluating models, and improving them much easier, so teams could build models that work well for their particular use case.

r001.rationale: The response says data quality affects model behavior, but does not identify data practices as the primary driver of Bard’s improvement during his time on the extended team.

r002.rationale: It describes making data creation and evaluation easier, but does not mention Google’s tools being inaccessible externally as an unmet need.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes high-quality training data without comparing its returns to tuning model hyperparameters.

r004.rationale: It does not mention DataComp or describe holding the model fixed while optimizing data.
